description: We chose the Challenge on Earth analogs for Moon and Mars, because crews and habitats need testing on Earth before launch, yet real analog sites are scarce and costly. We scored every 6 km tile of Earth against planned lunar and Martian sites using NASA data, a weighted similarity model, and Monte Carlo uncertainty, back-tested on known analogs. This open ranking helps scientists with small budgets conduct experiments near them, prove they qualify, enabling low-cost local research and training.
summary: GSOP is an open catalog of Earth places that people use, or could use, as stand-ins for Moon base and Mars sites. We built a catalog of 119 places in more than 30 countries and regions. Each place has a page with a photo or NASA satellite view, a facts table that links its sources, why it counts as an analog and where the analogy breaks down. A dashboard maps and ranks the places, Moon or Mars, with a World view and an India view, using a screening score built from NASA data. It addresses the challenge by answering place by place what makes an Earth site analogous and where the analogy fails. It matters because mission teams need somewhere on Earth to test first, and the usual list is a few famous sites. We show our failures first: the score failed three of its own pass-mark gates, so it is a lead, not a verdict. An India layer adds 15 places from published studies and asks for ground measurements. Every number on the site traces to a source file with a hash.
details:
What it does and how it works: GSOP has two layers. The catalog holds 119 places (120 entries, 60 for the Moon and 60 for Mars, 100 in our reference list and 20 candidates not in it). Each place page carries a summary, a photo with its credit or a NASA GIBS satellite view, more than 600 facts that link about 180 source pages, terrain and geology, climate, access, hazards, why it counts as an analog and where that stops, experiments proposed, and the score we stored for it. The Sites page searches and filters the catalog. The dashboard maps it, ranked by similarity, with a card for each place.

The screening layer cuts Earth's land into 3,972,955 equal-area 6 km tiles and compares each with two lunar south pole targets and Jezero crater on Mars. Only tiles that pass land-cover gates are scored (1,226,294 in the first Shackleton rim run). A Monte Carlo of 2,000 runs varies the weights. The second run added a MODIS land surface temperature layer.

Results, failures first: G1 (thermal coverage 73.4% against 85% required), G2 (Moon controls scored 58.2 and 38.0 against a maximum of 25; 0 of 4 scorable Mars sites reached the 95th percentile) and G3 failed. G2(c) passed but only shows the engine reproduces v1. D1, D2 and Moon recall were not tested. One thing improved: the held-out Moon false-positive rate fell from 21.4% to 1.0%. That is a description, not a passed test. The ranking has not been checked against independent data, and Mars is a low-confidence secondary result.

Benefits and intended impact: Mission and field-test planners get a sourced, searchable place to start. Researchers get open static data files with a claims file that names the source and hash of every number. Students and teachers get plain-language place pages. In India, the catalog flags 15 places from published reviews and studies and asks local teams for dated, located, instrument-based measurements, because ground data decides whether the 6 km satellite view is right. We claim no partnership with ISRO or any agency.

Tools:

  • Site: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and react-leaflet, a WebGL2 shader for the hero, hosted on Vercel.
  • Data build: Python (numpy, pyarrow, pyproj, PyYAML, Pillow), Google Earth Engine to read the NASA and Copernicus layers.
  • Checks: Vitest, GitHub Actions, and a claims check that fails the build on an unsourced number, a banned word or an altered uncertainty statement.
  • AI assistants: Claude Code and ChatGPT's image tool (see the AI-use answer).
  • Hardware: laptops only.

How it is creative: It is a failures-first catalog. The pass marks were written before the run, the uncertainty statement sits next to the results word for word, and a Failure-First Ledger lists where each analogy breaks. The India layer pairs a map with a concrete ask for ground data.

Factors the team considered: Honesty about limits, so we published the failures.

Reproducibility: every file is static and hashed, and the v1 results archive is shared on request.

Accessibility: contrast checked against WCAG AA in both themes and usable on a phone.

Privacy: no accounts or forms. Licences and credits for every dataset and photo. India, because that is where the team can reach ground data.
